t: A ball sits still at the top of a hill. It has not moved. What does it have?
A ball is at rest at the top of a hill. What does it have that a ball at the bottom does not?
A stationary ball at height h has something a stationary ball at ground level lacks. What is it?
A body at rest at height h possesses a quantity absent at h=0. Identify it.
sub: It is not moving. But it is high up. And that matters.
Height is not nothing. A ball at the top of a hill can do something a ball at the bottom cannot.
Position carries energy. The ball at height has potential — the capacity to move, once it falls.
Gravitational potential energy: U = mgh. A state function of position in a gravitational field.

question: A ball is twice as high. Does it have twice the height energy?
Double the height of a ball. Does its stored energy double?
If h → 2h, what happens to the potential energy?
If height doubles (at constant m and g), how does U change?
options: Yes, twice the height means twice the energy
No, the energy stays the same
No, the energy goes up by four
stages.outcome: Yes, twice the height means twice the energy
note: Guess before you try. The answer is simpler than you might think.
Predict. The relationship is one of the simplest in physics.
Form a hypothesis from U = mgh before testing.
Predict. U ∝ h at constant m, g. Verify in the sim.

t: Change the starting height. Watch the PE bar — higher start means more PE.
Set the start height to 2, then 4. Watch the PE bar (gold). Higher start = more potential energy.
goal: Launch the ball. Watch the PE bar shrink as it falls — that stored energy is becoming motion.
Launch. Observe PE → KE conversion as the ball descends. The PE bar shrinks; the KE bar grows.

t: Find the minimum start height to clear the hill. Then predict: does doubling the height double the speed at the bottom?
Determine the minimum h₀ to clear the hill. Then predict: if h₀ doubles, does v at the bottom double? (Hint: KE = ½mv², PE = mgh.) Test and verify.
goal: Clear the hill. The height you started with determined whether you made it.
Clear the hill. Verify energy conservation: mgh₀ = ½mv² at the bottom (minus friction).

t: Being high up gives a thing stored energy. That is called potential energy.
The energy of being high up is called potential energy. The higher you are, the more you have.
Potential energy (PE) is the energy of position. For gravity, PE = mgh — mass times gravity times height.
Gravitational potential energy: U = mgh. A state function of position in a gravitational field. The reference height is arbitrary; only ΔU is physically meaningful.
sub: When the ball falls, the potential energy turns into the energy of moving. That is the trade.
Potential energy converts to kinetic energy as the ball falls. PE at the top = KE at the bottom (no friction).
PE = mgh. At the bottom, all PE has converted to KE = ½mv². So mgh = ½mv², giving v = √(2gh).
Conservation of mechanical energy: mgh₀ = ½mv² + mgh. The total is constant in the absence of non-conservative forces.

t: A dam holds water high up. The water's potential energy is what makes electricity when it falls.
Hydroelectric dams use potential energy. Water at height has PE; as it falls, PE becomes KE, which spins turbines.
A hydroelectric dam is a PE-to-KE-to-electrical converter. Hoover Dam: water drops 180 m, generating 2 GW.
Hydroelectric power: P = ηρgQh, where Q is flow rate and h is head. The gravitational potential energy of stored water is the largest form of grid-scale energy storage worldwide.

options: The energy of being high up
why: Potential energy is the energy of position. A ball at the top of a hill has it; a ball at the bottom does not. The higher you go, the more you have.
Potential energy is stored energy of position. For gravity, PE = mgh. A ball at height h has mgh of stored energy that can be released by falling.
Gravitational PE = mgh. It is the work gravity would do if the body fell from h to the reference level. A state function of position.
U = mgh is the gravitational potential energy in a uniform field. It represents the capacity to do work as the body descends. Only ΔU is measurable; the zero is arbitrary.

q: Ball A is at height 2. Ball B is at height 4. Who has more potential energy?
Ball A is at h=2, Ball B at h=4. Which has more PE?
Two balls of equal mass: A at h=2, B at h=4. Which has greater U?
Two identical masses at h₁=2 and h₂=4. Which has greater gravitational PE?
options: Ball B — twice the height means twice the PE
why: PE = mass × gravity × height. Same ball, same gravity. Double the height, double the PE. Ball B has twice as much.
PE = mgh. With m and g constant, PE ∝ h. Ball B at h=4 has twice the PE of Ball A at h=2.
U = mgh. At constant m, g: U ∝ h. U_B = 2 × U_A.
U = mgh is linear in h. U_B/U_A = h_B/h_A = 4/2 = 2. The relationship is direct proportionality.
